en: Giving AI agents ways of verifying their
work on their own, like automated tests or
browser access, is very useful.
You can kind of take that to the extreme by
building a loop where you essentially don't
interact with Claude code at all anymore.
And that pattern is also known as the Rolf
loop.
It's named after Rolf Wiggum, the character
from The Simpsons for its naive persistence.
The ultimate idea behind that Ralph loop is
pretty simple. You create a shell script and
you find this updated starting project
including the shell script attached in case
you wanna try it.
And that shell script in the end sets up a
loop,
a loop that goes through a maximum amount of
iterations specified by you. And that
maximum amount of iterations is simply
an input that's expected to ensure that the
loop doesn't keep on running
but that it has some exit condition.
But whilst the loop is running, Claude code
is invoked over and over again
with all permissions allowed and therefore
you should configure it to run in sandbox
mode, more on that in a second.
And we're not running Claude code in the
interactive mode in which we used it
throughout the course but instead with the
-p flag, we can pass in a prompt directly.
And the prompt we do pass in is this one
here where we point at some files, which
I'll show you in a second, and where we then
ask Claude Code to pick a task from a list
of tasks
where passes is set to false, and you'll see
that list in a second,
and where we then wanted to tackle that task
and also verify its changes by running tests
and by also visiting the website by using
the Playwright MCP. So by testing those
changes in the browser as you saw over the
last lectures. Now, that list of tasks is
simply a JSON document with a bunch of
tasks, and the format is totally up to you.
This will be handled by an AI, so there is
no fixed format. This is just one convention
you often see,
that you have a description of the task,
some steps that make up the task, and a
passes flag, which initially is set to false
for all tasks. And the idea is that the
agent changes it to true task by task once
it worked through them. Through the tasks.
The idea is also that the agent doesn't have
to go in order but chooses on its own the
next task it should tackle.
Now, this task list in my case here was
derived from this spec document which I
created early on in this course.
And I used AI for deriving this list of
tasks here. And you can of course define any
tasks you want and be as granular as you
want.
You should try to not be too granular or too
general though. The tasks should typically
be focusing on one main problem each.
But then the idea is really just that you
keep Claude Code running on its own task by
task and that it verifies its work on its
own with tests, with browser access, and you
as a human don't do anything. You keep
Claude working and you come back once it's
done to verify the overall result. That's
the idea. Now, important, you have to grant
Claude code
broad permissions because otherwise it would
need your permission to, for example, edit a
file or to send an HTTP request. And the
idea is that it can go on its own. So since
that's the case, you must make sure that you
got this sandbox mode enabled.
You could also try running Docker sandbox
here, run Claude with Docker sandbox, which
I also showed you earlier. But I
consistently ran into various problems there
when it, for example, example came to Claude
Code trying to use the browser, which is why
I'm using this built-in sandbox mode
instead.
